title: When Should You See a GP About Arthritis?

content:
See your GP if joint pain, swelling or stiffness lasts more than a few weeks, if stiffness lasts more than 30 minutes in the morning, or if pain is stopping you working, sleeping or doing everyday tasks. Ask for an urgent appointment if several joints are swollen. A single hot, red, swollen joint with fever needs same-day help.

Signs to book a GP appointment

  • joint pain that has not improved after two weeks of self-care
  • swelling in one or more joints
  • stiffness in the morning lasting more than 30 minutes
  • pain in the small joints of the hands or feet, especially on both sides
  • back pain that started before 45, has lasted over three months and is worse with rest and better with movement
  • joint pain with psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, rashes, dry eyes or mouth ulcers
  • joint pain with tiredness, weight loss or feeling unwell
  • pain that wakes you at night
  • difficulty with walking, stairs, dressing or gripping

Related reading: Osteoarthritis Symptoms & When to See Your GP, Should You Tell Your Employer About Your Arthritis?

Why early appointments matter

For inflammatory arthritis, such as rheumatoid arthritis, early treatment can prevent permanent joint damage. NICE (NG100) recommends urgent referral to a rheumatologist for people with persistent joint swelling, particularly in the hands and feet, or where symptoms have lasted three months or more.

For osteoarthritis, early advice on exercise, weight and pain relief can make symptoms easier to manage.

If you already have arthritis

Contact your GP or rheumatology team if:

  • you have a flare that does not settle with your usual plan
  • you develop new swollen joints
  • you have side effects from medicines
  • your pain relief is not working
  • you are struggling with mood, sleep or work
  • you are thinking about pregnancy, surgery or travel and take arthritis medicines

Many rheumatology teams have an advice line for people already under their care.

When to use NHS 111

Use NHS 111, online or by phone, if you need urgent advice and are not sure where to go, for example if:

  • a joint is suddenly very swollen and painful
  • you have a fever while on immune-suppressing medicines
  • you have a painful red eye with blurred vision and have inflammatory arthritis

Other routes to help

  • pharmacists can advise on pain relief, gels and medicine interactions without an appointment
  • NHS physiotherapy often accepts self-referrals for joint and muscle problems
  • NHS 111 online can help you decide what to do

Preparing for your GP appointment

  • list your symptoms, which joints are affected and when they started
  • note how long morning stiffness lasts
  • take photos of swollen joints, in case swelling has gone down
  • list your medicines and supplements
  • think about how symptoms affect your daily life and work
  • write down your questions
  • note family history of arthritis, psoriasis or autoimmune conditions

What your GP may do

Your GP will examine your joints and may arrange blood tests, X-rays or a referral to physiotherapy or rheumatology. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed without tests. If you are referred, ask how long you might wait and what to do if your symptoms get worse in the meantime.

If you feel you are not being heard

If your symptoms are not improving, ask for a review. You can ask to see a different GP, or ask whether a referral is appropriate. Keeping a symptom diary can help show how things are changing over time.

Remember that you are not wasting anyone's time by getting joint symptoms checked. Early advice often means simpler treatment and a better outcome. If you are unsure whether your symptoms need a GP, a pharmacist or NHS 111 online can help you decide.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
